summary.text: Strong induction on the number of monochromatic edges in a Boolean coloring shows that every finite non-3-colorable graph has some bounded edge set \(Q\) on which every Boolean coloring has at least \(k>0\) monochromatic edges: a lower-error coloring is repaired in a ball and glued through a clean four-level annulus using a third color, while otherwise bounded walk covers and finite branching produce \(Q\). Choosing a divergent \(f\) so slowly that \(f(n)<k\) up to the number of endpoints of each such certificate makes the profile bound impossible for any non-3-colorable finite subgraph—bipartizing the endpoint set would have to delete all its at least \(k\) monochromatic certificate edges—and finite-color compactness then forces the whole graph to be 3-colorable.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the universally quantified assertion by constructing a particular function
\(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) which tends to infinity, but for which every graph satisfying the stated profile bound is in fact 3-colorable. Such a graph cannot have infinite chromatic number.

Throughout, a Boolean coloring means a map to \(\{0,1\}\). If \(G\) is a finite graph and \(c\) is a Boolean coloring of its vertices, write
\[
   \operatorname{Bad}_G(c)=\{xy\in E(G):c(x)=c(y)\}.
\]
Thus deleting \(\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)\) makes \(c\) a proper Boolean coloring. Conversely, if deleting an edge set \(E\) makes a finite graph bipartite, a proper Boolean coloring of the resulting graph has all of its monochromatic edges in \(E\). In particular,
\[
  |\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)|\le |E|.
\]
For a finite edge set \(Q\), let \(\partial Q\) denote the set of all endpoints of edges in \(Q\). We always have
\[
  |\partial Q|\le 2|Q|.
\]

We shall use the following kind of certificate. A \(k\)-certificate in a graph \(G\) is a finite edge set \(Q\subseteq E(G)\) such that every Boolean coloring \(d\) of \(V(G)\) makes at least \(k\) edges of \(Q\) monochromatic. The main finite result is this.

**Finite certificate theorem.** There is a sequence of natural numbers \(N(k)\), independent of the graph, such that every finite graph which is not 3-colorable has, for some positive integer \(k\), a \(k\)-certificate \(Q\) satisfying
\[
  |Q|\le N(k).
\]

We first prove this theorem. Explicit bounds will be given, although only their finiteness and dependence on \(k\) matter in the final contradiction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Compressing bounded-radius parity constraints

We begin with a compression lemma. Let \(P\subseteq D\) be spanning graphs on the same vertex set. Suppose that:

1. \(c\) is a proper Boolean coloring of \(P\);
2. \(K\) is a finite set of roots;
3. every vertex \(v\) has a walk in \(P\), of length at most \(R\), from \(v\) to a chosen root \(r(v)\in K\).

Then there is a finite set \(Q\subseteq E(D)\) with
\[
  |Q|\le (2R+1)(2|K|)^2
\]
such that any Boolean coloring which is proper on every edge of \(Q\) yields a proper Boolean coloring of all of \(D\). Consequently, if \(D\) is not bipartite, every Boolean coloring has a monochromatic edge in \(Q\).

To prove this, assign to each vertex its signature
\[
   \sigma(v)=(r(v),c(v))\in K\times\{0,1\}.
\]
For every ordered pair \((\alpha,\beta)\) of signatures which is realized by some edge \(vw\in E(D)\), choose one such edge. Retain that edge together with all edges of the chosen \(P\)-walks from \(v\) and \(w\) to their roots. For an unrealized pair retain nothing. Let \(Q\) be the union of all retained edges. There are \((2|K|)^2\) ordered pairs of signatures, and each contributes at most \(2R+1\) edges, proving the size bound.

Now suppose \(d\) is proper on \(Q\). On a walk on which both \(c\) and \(d\) are proper, the Boolean quantity
\[
   d(x)\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}c(x)
\]
is constant: both colors flip across every edge. Define a color of a signature \((s,b)\) by
\[
   \widehat d(s,b)=d(s)\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}c(s)\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}b.
\]
Along the retained walk from \(v\) to \(r(v)\), constancy of \(d\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}c\) gives
\[
   \widehat d(\sigma(v))=d(v).
\]
If \(vw\) is the representative edge for a realized pair \((\alpha,\beta)\), then it belongs to \(Q\), so \(d(v)\ne d(w)\), and hence
\(\widehat d(\alpha)\ne\widehat d(\beta)\). It follows that
\(v\mapsto\widehat d(\sigma(v))\) properly colors every edge of \(D\). This proves the compression lemma.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Amplifying a one-edge obstruction

We need to amplify the conclusion “every coloring has one bad edge in a bounded set” to “every coloring has at least \(t\) bad edges in one bounded set.” The following elementary branching argument does this.

Let \(U\) be a set and let \(\operatorname{bad}(d,e)\) be a predicate depending on an object \(d\) and an element \(e\in U\). Suppose that whenever \(A\subseteq U\) has fewer than \(t\) elements, there is a set \(Q_A\subseteq U\setminus A\), with \(|Q_A|\le b\), such that for every \(d\), at least one element of \(Q_A\) is bad for \(d\). Then there is a single finite \(J\subseteq U\) such that every \(d\) has at least \(t\) bad elements in \(J\), and the size of \(J\) is bounded solely in terms of \(t,b\).

One explicit bound is obtained from
\[
  S(t,b,0)=t,\qquad S(t,b,j+1)=t+bS(t,b,j).
\]
The resulting set can be chosen with size at most \(S(t,b,t)\).

Indeed, start with a set \(A\) of already required bad elements and with \(|A|+j=t\). If \(j=0\), use \(A\) itself. If \(j>0\), choose \(Q_A\). For every \(e\in Q_A\), recursively construct the branch corresponding to \(A\cup\{e\}\), and take the union of all those branches together with \(A\). For any fixed \(d\), the hitting property selects an \(e\in Q_A\) which is bad for \(d\), so the branch through that \(e\) supplies \(t\) bad elements. The displayed recurrence bounds the union. Starting with \(A=\varnothing\) and \(j=t\) proves the assertion.

We apply this to edges, with “bad” meaning monochromatic under a Boolean coloring.

Suppose \(B\subseteq H\), the Boolean coloring \(c\) is proper on \(B\), and every vertex is connected in \(B\) by a walk of length at most \(R\) to a root in a set \(S\) with \(|S|\le 2t\). Assume also that deleting fewer than \(t\) edges never makes \(H\) bipartite. Define
\[
 b(t,R)=(2R+1)(8t)^2,
 \qquad
 C(t,R)=S(t,b(t,R),t).
\]
We claim that \(H\) has a \(t\)-certificate with at most \(C(t,R)\) edges.

For the branching oracle, let \(A\) be any set of fewer than \(t\) previously chosen edges. Delete \(A\) from both \(B\) and \(H\). A walk in \(B\) may encounter a deleted edge. Truncate it immediately before its first such edge. The resulting walk lies in \(B-A\), has not increased in length, and ends either at its old root or at an endpoint of an edge of \(A\). Thus \(B-A\) still has a radius-\(R\) walk cover whose root set is
\[
   S\cup\partial A.
\]
Its size is at most
\[
   2t+2|A|\le 4t.
\]
The coloring \(c\) remains proper on \(B-A\), while \(H-A\) is non-bipartite by assumption. The compression lemma supplies a set \(Q_A\subseteq E(H-A)\), of size at most
\[
 (2R+1)(2\cdot 4t)^2=b(t,R),
\]
such that every Boolean coloring has a monochromatic edge in \(Q_A\). Since \(Q_A\subseteq E(H-A)\), it is disjoint from \(A\). This is exactly the oracle required by the branching argument, which gives the claimed \(t\)-certificate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Certificates from balls around bad edges

For a graph \(G\), a set of roots \(S\), and a cap \(M\), define
\[
  \ell(v)=\min\bigl(M,\text{length of a shortest walk from }v\text{ to }S\bigr),
\]
where \(\ell(v)=M\) if no such walk exists. Then \(0\le\ell(v)\le M\), every root has level zero, and adjacent vertices have levels differing by at most one. With cap \(R+1\), the set
\[
  T=\{v:\ell(v)\le R\}
\]
is exactly the radius-\(R\) walk-neighborhood of \(S\).

Let \(G\) be finite, let \(c\) be a Boolean coloring, and suppose
\[
  |\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)|=t.
\]
Take \(S=\partial\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)\), define levels with cap \(R+1\), and let \(H=G[T]\). Suppose every Boolean coloring of \(H\) has at least \(t\) bad edges. We claim that \(G\) has a \(t\)-certificate of size at most \(C(t,R)\).

Let
\[
 B=(G-\operatorname{Bad}_G(c))[T].
\]
The restriction of \(c\) is proper on \(B\). Also \(|S|\le2t\). Every vertex of \(T\) has a \(G\)-walk of length at most \(R\) to \(S\). Truncate that walk just before its first edge in \(\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)\). It becomes a walk in \(G-\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)\), still ending at an element of \(S\). Every vertex on this truncated walk remains in \(T\), because its distance from the terminal root is no greater than the total walk length. Thus this is a walk in \(B\), and \(B\) has the required radius-\(R\) cover by at most \(2t\) roots.

The hypothesis that every Boolean coloring of \(H\) has at least \(t\) bad edges implies that no deletion of fewer than \(t\) edges can make \(H\) bipartite: otherwise a proper Boolean coloring after deletion would have fewer than \(t\) bad edges in \(H\). The result of the preceding section therefore gives a \(t\)-certificate in \(H\), of size at most \(C(t,R)\). Viewed as edges of \(G\), it is the desired ambient certificate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Gluing 3-colorings across four levels

The repair argument uses a simple four-level interpolation. Embed Boolean colors as colors \(0,1\) in a three-color palette \(\{0,1,2\}\). Suppose \(c,c_1\) are Boolean colorings. On a four-row band, indexed by \(i=0,1,2,3\), define a color \(B_i(c,c_1)\) as follows. If \(c=c_1\), use the common Boolean color on every row. If \(c\ne c_1\), the ordered pairs of colors for \(c=0\) and \(c=1\), respectively, are
\[
 egin{array}{c|cccc}
 i&0&1&2&3\\ \hline
 (B_i(0,1),B_i(1,0))&(1,0)&(2,0)&(2,1)&(0,1).
\end{array}
\]
Thus row zero agrees with \(c_1\), and row three agrees with \(c\).

A direct check of these four rows gives the following gluing fact. Let \(\ell:V(G)\to\mathbb N\) change by at most one along every edge, and fix \(a\). Suppose:

* \(\gamma\) is a proper 3-coloring on all edges whose endpoints have levels at most \(a\);
* \(c\) is a proper Boolean coloring on all edges whose endpoints have levels at least \(a\);
* \(c_1\) is proper on all edges lying wholly in the band \(a\le\ell\le a+3\);
* at level \(a\), \(\gamma\) agrees with the embedded coloring \(c_1\).

Keep \(\gamma\) below the band, keep the embedded \(c\) above it, and use
\[
 B_{\ell(v)-a}(c(v),c_1(v))
\]
in the band. This is a proper 3-coloring of \(G\).

For completeness, why does the finite row check suffice? On an edge in the band, the row indices differ by at most one. Since both \(c\) and \(c_1\) are proper there, both Boolean colors flip across the edge, so
\(c\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}c_1\) is unchanged. If this xor is zero, the two endpoints receive their distinct \(c\)-colors. If it is one, inspection of the four displayed pairs shows that neighboring rows also receive distinct colors. Edges wholly below or above the band are handled by \(\gamma\) or \(c\). An edge crossing a boundary is covered by the same formulas because row zero equals \(c_1\), row three equals \(c\), and levels change by at most one.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. The local repair induction

Define radii recursively by
\[
  r_0=0,
  \qquad
  r_t=(2t-1)(2r_{t-1}+4)\quad(t>0).
\]
These radii are nondecreasing. Set
\[
  N(t)=C(t,r_t).
\]
We prove, by strong induction on \(t\), the following alternative.

Let \(G\) be a finite graph and let \(c\) be a Boolean coloring with exactly \(t\) bad edges. Then either:

1. there is a proper 3-coloring \(\Gamma\) of \(G\) which agrees with the embedded coloring \(c\) at every vertex farther than \(r_t\) from the endpoints of \(\operatorname{Bad}_G(c)\); or
2. for some positive \(k\), the graph \(G\) has a \(k\)-certificate of size at most \(N(k)\).

When \(t=0\), \(c\) is already proper, so its embedding into three colors gives the first alternative.

Now let \(t>0\), and assume the result for all smaller values. Put
\[
 F=\operatorname{Bad}_G(c),\qquad S=\partial F,
\]
define capped levels from \(S\) with cap \(r_t+1\), and let
\[
 T=\{v:\ell(v)\le r_t\},\qquad H=G[T].
\]
There are two cases.

**Case 1.** Every Boolean coloring of \(H\) has at least \(t\) bad edges.

By the ball-certificate result of Section 3, \(G\) has a \(t\)-certificate of size at most \(C(t,r_t)=N(t)\). Since \(t>0\), this is the second alternative.

**Case 2.** Some Boolean coloring \(c_1\) of \(H\) has \(s<t\) bad edges.

Apply the induction hypothesis to \((H,c_1)\). If it produces a certificate in \(H\), the same edge set, viewed in \(G\), is a certificate with the same size and parameter, so again we obtain the second alternative.

It remains to consider the subcase in which induction produces a proper 3-coloring \(\gamma\) of \(H\) which agrees with embedded \(c_1\) outside the radius-\(r_s\) neighborhood, within \(H\), of the endpoints of \(\operatorname{Bad}_H(c_1)\). Since \(s\le t-1\) and the radii are nondecreasing,
\[
 r_s\le r_{t-1}.
\]
We will glue \(\gamma\) to \(c\).

We need a clean four-level annulus. Let
\[
 Z=\partial\operatorname{Bad}_H(c_1).
\]
Since \(c_1\) has at most \(t-1\) bad edges,
\[
 |Z|\le 2s\le 2t-2.
\]
Partition the positive levels into \(2t-1\) consecutive blocks of length
\(2r_{t-1}+4\). Each exceptional vertex \(z\in Z\) can obstruct at most one block in the following encoding: assign it the block containing \(\ell(z)-1\). There are at most \(2t-2\) obstructing vertices and \(2t-1\) blocks, so one block is unoccupied. In the center of such a block we can choose four consecutive levels
\[
  a,a+1,a+2,a+3
\]
which are more than \(r_{t-1}\) away, in level, from every \(\ell(z)\), and which satisfy
\[
  1\le a,
  \qquad
  a+3\le (2t-1)(2r_{t-1}+4)=r_t.
\]
More explicitly, if the unused block has index \(i\), beginning at \(i(2r_{t-1}+4)+1\), take
\[
 a=i(2r_{t-1}+4)+1+r_{t-1}.
\]
Then every level from \(a\) through \(a+3\) is separated from every exceptional level by more than \(r_{t-1}\).

Because level changes by at most one along an edge, and hence by at most the length of a walk, no vertex in this four-level annulus can be joined inside \(H\) to an element of \(Z\) by a walk of length at most \(r_{t-1}\). In particular it cannot be joined by a walk of length at most \(r_s\). Therefore, on the annulus, \(\gamma\) agrees with the embedded coloring \(c_1\).

We now verify the other hypotheses of the gluing lemma. The original coloring \(c\) is proper on every edge both of whose endpoints have positive level. Indeed, every bad edge of \(c\) has both endpoints in \(S\), hence at level zero. Since \(a\ge1\), \(c\) is proper on the whole exterior beginning at level \(a\).

Likewise, \(c_1\) is proper on every edge lying in the four-level annulus. If an annular endpoint belonged to an edge bad for \(c_1\), it would belong to \(Z\), and hence would be at distance zero from \(Z\), contradicting the separation just proved.

The coloring \(\gamma\) is proper throughout \(H\), so in particular below level \(a\). The entire annulus lies in \(T\), because \(a+3\le r_t\). Thus the gluing lemma applies and gives a proper 3-coloring \(\Gamma\) of all of \(G\), equal to embedded \(c\) on levels at least \(a+3\). Every vertex farther than \(r_t\) from \(S\) has capped level \(r_t+1\), and hence lies above the annulus. Therefore \(\Gamma\) agrees there with embedded \(c\). This is the first alternative and completes the strong induction.

Now take any finite graph \(G\) which is not 3-colorable. Begin with the constant Boolean coloring, and let \(t\) be its number of bad edges. Apply the local alternative. Its first outcome would itself be a proper 3-coloring of \(G\), impossible. Hence its second outcome supplies a positive \(k\) and a \(k\)-certificate \(Q\) with
\[
 |Q|\le N(k).
\]
This proves the finite certificate theorem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. A divergent budget lying below all certificate parameters

We next construct a very slowly divergent function. The construction works for any prescribed sequence \(L(k)\). Define the monotone, unbounded majorant
\[
  M(k)=k+1+\sum_{i=0}^{k}L(i).
\]
It satisfies \(L(k)\le M(k)\), is nondecreasing, and tends to infinity. Define
\[
  f(n)=\min\{j\in\mathbb N:n\le M(j+1)\}.
\]
The set is nonempty because the linear term in \(M\) eventually exceeds \(n\).

This \(f\) tends to infinity. Indeed, if \(n>M(k)\), then no \(j<k\) can satisfy \(n\le M(j+1)\), by monotonicity of \(M\). Hence \(f(n)\ge k\). Thus for every fixed \(k\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(f(n)\ge k\).

On the other hand, for every \(k\ge1\) and every \(n\le L(k)\),
\[
 n\le L(k)\le M(k)=M((k-1)+1),

to f(n)\le k-1<k.
\]

Apply this construction with
\[
  L(k)=2N(k).
\]
We have obtained a particular function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that
\[
 f(n)\longrightarrow\infty

to
after removing the accidental text “to”; explicitly, the conclusion is
\[
 f(n)\to\infty,
\]
and such that
\[
  k\ge1,
  \quad n\le 2N(k)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  f(n)<k.                                      \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. A certificate contradicts the profile bound

We relate certificates to the deletion profile in the problem.

Suppose a graph \(G\) satisfies
\[
  \operatorname{maxdist}_G(n)\le f(n)
  \qquad\text{for every }n,                    \tag{2}
\]
where \(\operatorname{maxdist}_G(n)\) is the supremum, over finite \(n\)-vertex subgraphs, of the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes the subgraph bipartite.

Let \(Q\subseteq E(G)\) be a \(k\)-certificate, and put \(S=\partial Q\). Consider the subgraph induced by \(S\). It is finite and has \(|S|\) vertices. By (2), it can be made bipartite by deleting a set \(E\) of at most \(f(|S|)\) edges. Choose a proper Boolean coloring \(d\) after this deletion. Every edge of \(Q\) has both endpoints in \(S\). Since \(Q\) is a \(k\)-certificate, at least \(k\) edges of \(Q\) are monochromatic under \(d\). Every such edge must have been deleted, because \(d\) is proper on the graph remaining after deletion. Consequently
\[
  k\le |E|\le f(|S|).                           \tag{3}
\]

This also explains directly why the minimum and supremum conventions in the profile cause no difficulty. On every finite subgraph, deleting all edges is an admissible finite bipartizing deletion, so the minimum exists. The set of distances for fixed \(n\) is bounded, for instance by \(n^2\), so its supremum is finite; and the particular induced subgraph on \(S\) has distance at most the ambient maximum. If there are no subgraphs of some size, the corresponding empty supremum is irrelevant to this argument.

Now let \(G\) be a finite graph satisfying (2). If it were not 3-colorable, the finite certificate theorem would give a positive \(k\) and a \(k\)-certificate \(Q\) with \(|Q|\le N(k)\). Hence
\[
  |\partial Q|\le2|Q|\le2N(k).
\]
By (1),
\[
  f(|\partial Q|)<k.
\]
But (3) says \(k\le f(|\partial Q|)\), a contradiction. We conclude:

> Every finite graph satisfying the profile bound (2) is 3-colorable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8. Compactness and the final contradiction

Finally let \(G\) be an arbitrary, possibly infinite, graph satisfying (2). Every finite induced subgraph \(H\) of \(G\) inherits the same profile bound: any finite subgraph of \(H\) is also a finite subgraph of \(G\), and an injective inclusion cannot increase the minimum bipartizing deletion distance beyond the corresponding ambient maximum. Thus every finite induced subgraph of \(G\) is 3-colorable by the finite result.

By the finite-coloring compactness theorem, \(G\) itself is 3-colorable. One standard proof is to consider the compact product space \(\{0,1,2\}^{V(G)}\). For each edge \(xy\), the condition that the colors of \(x\) and \(y\) differ is closed. Every finite collection of these conditions involves only a finite subgraph and is satisfiable by its 3-coloring. The finite intersection property therefore gives a point satisfying all edge conditions, namely a proper 3-coloring of \(G\).

Thus every graph whose profile is bounded by our particular divergent function \(f\) has chromatic number at most \(3\), and in particular does not have infinite chromatic number.

The conjectured statement asserted that for every function tending to infinity, including this \(f\), there exists a graph of infinite chromatic number satisfying the profile bound. For this \(f\) no such graph exists. Therefore the stated formalization of Erdős problem 74 is false.
